title: The Hedgehog Who Worried Too Much
markdown:
Eli the hedgehog kept the Whispering Woods Historical Museum as if acorns could take offence at a crooked label. His quills buzzed faster than dandelion seed. Today the quiet had fluttered off: a century-mark photograph by Willow Creek, near the old school boathouse. Light must be right. Placement symmetrical. And Ren must stand exactly there.

Ren the hare, ears long, spirit startling, represented Friends of the Creek. He was maddeningly competent. Eli had sketched a hierarchy to highlight the museum. Ren disrupted it by existing, easy smile and all.

“Still fretting?” chirped Nora, his neighbour, eyes like river stones. “You look as if you’ve swallowed a thistle.”

“This photograph must be definitive. Ren defies arrangement. He makes competence look like charm.”

Nora chuckled, pebbles on a lake. “You’re reaching for grand ambitions when you have one simple promise. The moonflower seeds?”

He had said he would plant them tonight, under the full moon. It had slipped. “The moonflowers. I had…”

“Allowed the grand to overshadow the small.” She nudged him. “I’ll manage the planting. You go be photographed.”

The boathouse smelled of damp wood and wild mint. Students buzzed. Ren stood near the photographer, a portly badger in a bright blue waistcoat. Eli’s diagram felt laughable. He arranged his spines. Ren winked into place.

“A slight draught,” said the badger, nodding at the propped door.

A gust snaked in. Fairy lights on the rafters trembled. Eli’s heart leaped. Ren strode over, snagged a trailing vine, secured the lights, and offered the photographer a calm “Nature’s little surprises.”

Eli’s chest went hollow. He had been so busy controlling the picture that he had missed help offered freely. It was not rivalry. It was competence without a diagram.

Later the moon, a pearl, silvered the creek. Eli sat in Nora’s garden. The moonflowers opened like white trumpets. He had not planted them; she had kept his promise for him, and still made room on the bench.

“I was trying to outshine Ren. I almost forgot everything else.”

Nora only gestured at the blooms. He looked, and the photograph’s cage loosened. The museum would still have its picture. The flowers, which asked for presence rather than hierarchy, had it. A moth tested the nearest trumpet and found nectar. Eli’s quills, for once, were still.
characters: Eli (a hedgehog museum guide), Nora (a hare neighbour)
audience: young adults aged 16-18, teen anthology entry
author: StoryGen Community
